title: Sausage Sandwich
subtitle: Fried pork sausages in soft white bread with ketchup
excerpt: Pork sausages fried until golden all over, put into soft white bread with ketchup or brown sauce. A weekend breakfast and post-match staple across Britain.
sourceNotes: Sausage sandwiches are documented in British canteen and working-breakfast records from the early twentieth century. Nigel Slater, Appetite (2000), informal reference for the sausage sandwich as a comfort meal. Recipe developed from first principles.

content.text: A sausage sandwich is fried pork sausages in soft white bread with ketchup. The sausages need to be cooked gently so the skin does not split before the centre is done. Start them in a cold pan: they render their own fat as the heat builds, which keeps them moist and colours the skin evenly.

Put {{sausages-pork}} sausages in a cold frying pan over medium-low heat. Cook for 12 to 15 minutes, turning every 3 to 4 minutes, until golden all over with no pink in the middle when cut. Do not prick the sausages.
While the sausages cook, butter {{bread-white}} slices if using and add the sauce to one side of each pair.
Lay 3 sausages on each base slice. Close the sandwich and press lightly. Serve hot.

rows.cause: Heat too high or sausages pricked before or during cooking
rows.fix: Never prick sausages. Start them in a cold pan and keep the heat at medium-low throughout.

rows.symptom: Sausages are golden outside but raw inside
rows.cause: Cooked too fast at too high a heat
rows.fix: Lower the heat and cook for longer. A sausage needs at least 12 minutes over medium-low heat to cook all the way through.

rows.cause: Sausages transferred to bread while dripping with fat
rows.fix: Rest the sausages on a piece of kitchen paper for 20 seconds before putting them in the bread.

rows.cause: Pan overcrowded so sausages stewed rather than fried
rows.fix: Fry in a single layer with space between them so the heat can circulate.

content.text: The sausage sandwich is a weekend breakfast and sporting-event staple across Britain. It appears in the same setting as the bacon sandwich but has its own strong identity, partly because of the range of British regional sausages: Cumberland, Lincolnshire, Newmarket, Glamorgan. The standard at home is a simple pork banger in white bread, but the particular type of sausage used is often a point of some pride.
